claims.text: The initial eutectic HEA consists of an FCC matrix and ordered B2 precipitates with fine-scale coherent phase boundaries.
Intermediate thermal aging drives the evolution of local chemical order within the B2 phase.
Intermediate thermal aging changes FCC/B2 phase boundaries from coherent to semi-coherent or incoherent.
At lower aging temperatures, local chemical orders nucleate and grow.
Growth of local chemical order increases the anti-phase-boundary energy.
Lower-temperature aging creates a high density of small, coherent B2 domains or precipitates.
Small coherent B2 domains force dislocations to cut ordered domains as single dislocations or pairs, thereby generating anti-phase boundaries.
High anti-phase-boundary energy can strengthen an HEA containing ordered precipitates.
Dislocation hindrance can produce hardening together with reduced ductility in an HEA.
High anti-phase-boundary energy and dislocation pile-ups at FCC/B2 phase boundaries cause the dramatic ductility loss.
Increasing aging temperature coarsens the ordered B2 domains.
Coarsening decreases the anti-phase-boundary density per unit volume.
Coarsened B2 domains permit dislocation bypass by Orowan looping or cross-slip.
The transition from dislocation cutting to bypass restores ductility at higher aging temperatures.
The embrittlement is caused by ordered-domain strengthening and phase-boundary evolution rather than impurity segregation or grain-boundary embrittlement.
The embrittlement regime spans approximately 400-700 degrees Celsius.
The transition out of the brittle regime occurs when the B2 domain size exceeds approximately 50-100 nm.
Ductility will fall by more than 50% around 500-600 degrees Celsius.
Above approximately 700 degrees Celsius, ductility will recover to more than 80% of its initial value.
The brittle regime will show increased yield strength and decreased fracture strain.

contradictions.description: The initial high-ductility state is described as already containing fine coherent B2 domains, while the mechanism also identifies a high density of small coherent B2 domains as forcing dislocation cutting and causing brittle fracture. The additional microstructural distinction that makes the aged coherent state brittle is not clearly specified.

The boundary labels the full 400-700 degrees Celsius interval as the embrittlement regime, whereas the predicted outcome places the pronounced brittle interval at 500-600 degrees Celsius and recovery only above about 700 degrees Celsius.
